newsitem.title: ITALY: San Paolo details top offer price.
newsitem.headline: San Paolo details top offer price.

text.p: Italian bank San Paolo di Torino announced the maximum price for its public share offer starting next week and an architect of its privatisation said at the weekend the move would make it an Anglo-Saxon style company.
San Paolo, Italy's biggest bank, announced late on Friday the maximum price at its public share issue would be 10,850 lire per share ($6.50).

The Turin-based bank, which is making a global offer of 26.96 percent of its capital, or 220 million ordinary shares, also said there would a 2.5 percent discount to the public in the offer which begins on Monday and runs until Friday.

The final price, which will be set at the end of the public offer period, will be whichever is the lowest between the 10,850 lire maximum price and the official price registered on the Milan stock market on Friday minus the 2.5 percent discount.
San Paolo shares closed on the stock market at 11,114 lire per ordinary share on Friday.
Analysts had forecast the final price to be somewhere in the region of 10,300 to 10,500 lire, saying the closer it is to 10,000 the more interested international investors will be.
Pricing for the offer is deemed critical in a banking sector which lags behind some of its European counterparts in terms of financial returns.
San Paolo, which has made big changes in the last 18 months ahead of privatisation, shows a return on equity of 6.1 percent compared to double-digit levels at British and German banks.

But Claudio Sposito, managing director of Morgan Stanley bank here and architect of the sale along with San Paolo chairman Gianni Zandano, told a newspaper on Saturday: "It will be a bank open to the market, private and managed on the model of public companies of the Anglo-Saxon type."

Sposito, whose bank has been global coordinator for the operation along with San Paolo, told Il Sole 24 Ore financial daily that the privatisation model they had chosen guaranteed there would be no surprises.
"Unlike operations carried out in the past, today the market knows already who San Paolo's stable shareholders are," he said.
"(The market) knows no one has a dominant position and it knows that among the members of the stable group there are no agreements which presuppose anyone acting in concert," he said.
Many large Italian companies quoted on the stock market have shareholder syndicates which vote or act together.
Sposito said that nevertheless the presence of big investors would act on the bank's management as a stimulus to provide a return on equity which would satisfy shareholders.

The foundation that controls San Paolo has already conducted a private placing of a 20 percent stake to a stable core of shareholders including Spain's Banca Santander and Italian investment bank IMI, bringing its own stake in San Paolo down to 45.6 percent from 65.6 percent.
San Paolo's sell-off is attracting more notice from abroad.

Hungarian financier George Soros, famous for betting against the British pound in a currency crisis in 1992, said on Italian television on Friday: "The privatisation of San Paolo could be a good investment, given that it's dealing with a very respectable institution."
However he did not say if he intended to invest. $1=1,672 lire
